clue.text: Government marks potential gold-seekers ?

definitions.meaning: the broad arrow stamped on British government property, once on convicts' uniforms
in archery the centre of the target is the gold, which every shot aims for

explanation.walkthrough: The 'gold-seekers' are not prospectors: in archery the bullseye is called the gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad-arrow stamps mark state property, and shafts loosed at a target each hope to strike its golden centre.

clue.text: Bird imitator of elementary skill ?

parts.note: air is one of the four classical elements, so elementary here means of an element
craft means skill or art

explanation.surface: A mimic of birdsong with only basic ability.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elementary' looks like basic; it means 'of an element', and air is one of the classical four.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane copies a bird by flying, imitating its winged flight through the sky.

clue.text: Interpretation of a county town

definitions.meaning: a construal, how someone understands a text or event
the county town of Berkshire, west of London

explanation.walkthrough: A county town is the administrative centre of an English county; this one is Berkshire's.
explanation.definitionFit: One's take on a text is how one construes it, and the same word names Berkshire's administrative centre.

clue.text: 1. P-K4 used by painters

definitions.meaning: in old chess notation, the first move, pawn to king's four, is made by the side with the pale pieces
a lead carbonate pigment once common in paint

explanation.surface: A chess opening move that painters rely on.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess the pale pieces always move first, so '1. P-K4' (pawn to king four, the first move in old descriptive notation) is that side opening the game. The pigment is a toxic lead carbonate once used in paint.
explanation.definitionFit: The side with the pale pieces makes the opening move in chess, and the same phrase names a lead carbonate pigment in old paints.

clue.text: A scholastic expansion went ahead

definitions.meaning: in British schooling the A of A level stands for this word

explanation.surface: Some school enlargement has gone ahead as planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is not a link word here: in British schools an A level is the advanced-level exam taken at about 18, so the letter A expands to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The A in the British exam name A level is short for this word, which also means progressed or moved forward.

clue.text: An idiotic male's reform of currency

definitions.text: An idiotic male's reform of currency

indicators.note: a reform reshapes something, so the letters of the phrase are reshaped into a new word

explanation.surface: A foolish man's plan to overhaul the money system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform of' rearranges the fourteen letters of AN IDIOTIC MALES. The whole clue is the definition too: Britain's switch to decimal money in 1971 was much mocked.
explanation.definitionFit: Converting money to a base-ten system, as Britain did in 1971 when shillings and old pence disappeared.

clue.text: Worry is negative in any case

indicators.note: in places the letter inside the word that follows it
the case is the outer word enclosing the letter like a box

parts.note: to say no is to be negative, to refuse

explanation.surface: Fretting is pointless whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in any case' reads as 'anyway'; here 'in' and 'case' put NO (from 'is negative') inside ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: To worry or pester someone is to bother or irritate them.

clue.text: Heading for arrest

definitions.meaning: a title above a picture or article
an old legal sense, the seizing of a person or goods

explanation.surface: Bound for arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading for' reads as 'going towards'; it is two definitions. The arrest sense is old legal usage (Latin captio, a seizing).
explanation.definitionFit: A title above a picture or article; in old legal usage the same word meant the seizure of a person.

clue.text: Dug 55 indeed !

indicators.note: in places the number inside the word printed right after it

parts.note: deed is taken as written
LV is 55 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An exclamation: someone dug, really!
explanation.walkthrough: 'indeed' splits into 'in' and 'deed': LV (55) goes in DEED.
explanation.definitionFit: To delve is to dig, so the past tense means dug.

clue.text: Put pedagogues in railway posts

parts.note: to station something is to put it in place
schoolmasters, here masters

explanation.surface: Give teachers jobs on the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put' is an instruction in the surface but supplies STATION, to place.
explanation.definitionFit: Officials in charge of railway stations hold those posts, so they are the people in railway posts.

clue.text: Curiously it is clear and practical

indicators.note: curiously means in an odd way, so the following words appear oddly rearranged

explanation.surface: Strangely, it is plain and sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curiously' rearranges the nine letters of IT IS CLEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A practical person or plan is sensible and grounded in facts, which is what a down-to-earth outlook means.

clue.text: A kingdom for a mount- Sir George's

definitions.text: A kingdom for a mount- Sir George's

parts.words: A kingdom for a mount- Sir George's
parts.note: echoes Richard III's 'my kingdom for a horse', but the mount here is a mountain named after the surveyor Sir George Everest, and the kingdom is the Himalayan land it stands in

explanation.surface: A king offers his realm in exchange for Sir George's horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' suggests a horse, as in Shakespeare's 'my kingdom for a horse'; it is Mount Everest, named after Sir George Everest, which stands on this country's border. It was a kingdom when the clue was set.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan country, a monarchy until 2008, contains Everest, the peak named after the surveyor Sir George Everest.

clue.text: Change in a 'term investment

indicators.note: change means alter, so the three words after it have their letters altered in order

explanation.surface: A switch in a fixed-term investment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' rearranges IN A TERM. 'Investment' is not money: it is the old sense of vesting, clothing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Investment in the old sense is the act of clothing someone, and raiment is clothing or apparel.

clue.text: When January's Chaucerian wife meets Hodgson's old gypsy man

parts.note: in Chaucer's Merchant's Tale old January marries young May
Ralph Hodgson's poem 'Time, You Old Gipsy Man' addresses Time

explanation.surface: A literary meeting of a character from Chaucer and a figure from a Hodgson poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Two literary references: May is the young wife of January in Chaucer's Merchant's Tale, and Ralph Hodgson's poem is 'Time, You Old Gipsy Man'. 'meets' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a season of the year, so it can stand for a time, answering a question beginning with when.

clue.text: Barred sonic flight?

parts.note: a piece of music written in bars, whose name comes from the Latin fuga, flight

explanation.surface: A supersonic flight that has been banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barred' looks like banned; it means written in musical bars. The form's name comes from Latin fuga, flight, because the voices seem to chase one another.
explanation.definitionFit: A contrapuntal musical composition where voices enter in turn, its name derived from the Latin word for flight.

clue.text: Anoints with pitch — may contribute to keenness

parts.note: to anoint is to smear with oil
the pitch of a sound is its tone

explanation.surface: A priest anointing with tar, said to sharpen the faithful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keenness' is the sharpness of a blade, not enthusiasm.
explanation.definitionFit: A whetstone lubricated with oil is used to hone blades, giving them a keen edge.

clue.text: Pedal percussion artiste

parts.note: a performer who makes rhythm with the feet, not a drummer working a pedal

explanation.surface: A drummer who works the bass pedal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedal' suggests a drum kit's foot pedal; it means 'of the feet', making a rhythm with metal-tipped shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A dancer with metal-tipped shoes beats out rhythms with the feet, making percussion through footwork.

clue.text: That's my boy-or rather his boy

definitions.text: That's my boy-or rather his boy

parts.words: That's my boy-or rather his boy
parts.note: the proud parent's cry, corrected to the child of the parent's son; also a fine son, a grand one

explanation.surface: A proud father corrects himself: the lad is his son's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's my boy' is a proud parent's cry, and a 'grand son' is a fine one; corrected to 'his boy', it is the son of one's son.
explanation.definitionFit: A son's son, the male child of one's child.

clue.text: Foreign address for ladies or a lady in a mess

indicators.note: in places the lady inside the mess, wrapped by it

parts.note: a mess is a muddle or shambles
a dame is a lady, also a British title for women

explanation.surface: How the French greet women, or a woman in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts DAME inside MESS, giving MES-DAME-S.
explanation.definitionFit: The French plural form of address for women, the equivalent of 'ladies' in a speech's opening.

clue.text: Avengers of Ireland given the go-ahead

parts.note: Erin is a poetic name for Ireland
yes gives permission, the go-ahead

explanation.surface: Irish vengeance-seekers are given permission to act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avengers of Ireland' looks like one phrase; 'of' is a link word, with the definition before it. The answer is the Greek name for the Furies.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek Furies, goddesses who pursued and punished wrongdoers, especially murderers of kin.

clue.text: One who takes steps to help another

definitions.text: One who takes steps to help another

parts.words: One who takes steps to help another
parts.note: a runner who sets the speed for another competitor in a race

explanation.surface: Someone who acts to assist a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes steps' sounds like taking action; it is literal running, setting the speed for another athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: In athletics a pacemaker runs alongside to set a steady speed for a rival or teammate.

clue.text: Marked with an X. like a T

definitions.meaning: an X is two lines over each other, as when ticking a ballot
a capital T has a horizontal stroke over its upright

explanation.walkthrough: One writes 'dot the i's and cross the t's': the bar across a T is its cross.
explanation.definitionFit: An X is two strokes intersecting, and a written T has its upright struck through by a bar.

clue.text: Flying phenomenon of China

definitions.meaning: a disc-shaped UFO, named after the dish it resembles
crockery: the dish under a teacup is part of a china set

explanation.surface: A UFO spotted over China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country; it is crockery. 'of' is a link word between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A small dish under a teacup, part of a china set, which also names a disc-shaped UFO.

clue.text: Flies with a seat arrangement to hold six

indicators.note: to hold means the rearranged letters surround the number inside them
an arrangement of the words a seat puts its letters in a new order

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Airline travel with a seating plan for six passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges A SEAT to AATES, and 'to hold' puts VI inside, after the first A.
explanation.definitionFit: To aviate is to pilot or travel in an aircraft, so the verb means flies.

clue.text: Tom the lift worker ?

parts.note: a digit raised by hitchhikers seeking a lift, and the first name of the folk-tale tiny hero Tom

explanation.surface: Tom who operates the elevator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lift worker' suggests a lift attendant; it is the digit hitchhikers raise to get a lift. Tom Thumb is the tiny hero of an English folk tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The digit a hitchhiker sticks out to ask for a ride, and the surname of the tiny hero of an English folk tale.

clue.text: Is it worn in the afternoon to make a stir ?

definitions.text: Is it worn in the afternoon to make a stir

parts.words: Is it worn in the afternoon to make a stir
parts.note: a loose dress for afternoon tea, which is the drink one might stir

explanation.surface: Is that outfit worn to cause a sensation at an afternoon party?
explanation.walkthrough: 'make a stir' suggests causing a sensation; one stirs a cup of tea at the afternoon meal this garment was made for.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose, elegant dress worn by Victorian and Edwardian women when receiving guests for afternoon tea.

clue.text: Modest back-up display by a furry creature

parts.note: coy means shy or modest

indicators.note: back tells us the word that follows is to be read in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A shy animal making a bashful show of support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns UP into PU, which follows COY. 'display by a' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American rodent with thick fur is farmed for its pelt, known as nutria.

clue.text: Dispiriting ceremonies

parts.note: read literally, rites that remove spirits from a possessed person

explanation.surface: Depressing formal occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispiriting' looks like depressing; read as dis-spiriting it means driving spirits out.
explanation.definitionFit: Rituals performed by priests to expel demons from the possessed drive the spirits out.

clue.text: One of those blooming old English shrubs perhaps

definitions.text: One of those blooming old English shrubs perhaps

parts.words: One of those blooming old English shrubs perhaps
parts.note: a flowering plant, the national flower of England, read with 'blooming' as a British mild oath

explanation.surface: An exasperated remark about one of those wretched traditional plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blooming' reads as a mild British swear word (as in 'one of those blooming things') but is meant literally: the shrub is in flower. The flower in question is England's emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowering shrub that bears England's national flower, an old garden favourite.

clue.text: 'The bells they sound on —' (Housman)

parts.note: a line from A. E. Housman's A Shropshire Lad, completed by the name of a Worcestershire hill

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Housman's poem 'Bredon Hill' in A Shropshire Lad begins 'In summertime on Bredon, the bells they sound so clear', and later 'The bells they sound on Bredon'. Bredon Hill is in Worcestershire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Housman's line is the name of a hill in Worcestershire whose church bells the poem describes.
